newsitem.title: POLAND: OPINION - NOBE institute Polish quarterly forecast.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - NOBE institute Polish quarterly forecast.

text.p: Following is a quarterly macroeconomic forecast commissioned by Reuters from Poland's Independent Centre for Economic Research (NOBE). ***************************************************************

Economic developments during first three quarters of 1996 were generally in line with the earlier expectations. The economic growth has bottomed in the third quarter and is likely to speed up slightly in the next two or three quarters. However, political uncertainties and some possible negative effects of next year's electoral campaign may cause a slowdown again in the second half of 1997 despite an assumed more favourable external environment.

Four main factors influenced the economic performance of Poland in the first three quarters of 1996. First, the growth of exports was slowing, mainly due to the slow growth of the West European demand. Second, the pace of imports remained above the expected levels, as a result of high growth rates of the domestic absorption (mainly booming gross fixed capital formation) combined with the real appreciation of the zloty (forced by increased capital inflows). Third, the growth rate of the personal consumption remained stable despite the slight acceleration of the CPI inflation caused by food market fluctuations. Four, the fixed investment was growing even faster than expected, indicating continuation of the process of fast retooling of the Polish industry. All the above phenomena will be also observed in the four coming quarters, albeit some trends may be modified or even reversed. The main factors influencing the economic situation will be:
EXPORTS TO GROW FASTER IN 1997 ON PICKUP IN WESTERN DEMAND

1. Fast growth of both exports and imports. However, as import growth rate will remain much higher than the growth of exports, the trade deficit will increase. A moderate appreciation pressure will continue mainly due to strong capital inflows. The rate of growth of imports will fall slowly while the exports will accelerate in 1997 mainly due to the more favourable external environment (acceleration of the growth in Western Europe)

2. Continuously high growth of the fixed capital investment. The roots of the high investment dynamics are deep and only partly dependent on the business cycle. The economy will continue the retooling process, searching for higher competitiveness in prospects of an eventual free access to the EU market by the end of the century. However, uncertainties caused by the general elections due late in 1997 may result in some slowdown of the dynamics of investment.

3. Easing infationary pressure, mainly due to continuously falling industrial prices. The drop of the CPI inflation will be relatively modest in 1996 (due to a relatively high food prices' growth). CPI inflation is likely to slow down again in the first quarters of 1997.

4. Stabilizing role played by the consumption. The personal consumption boom will continue, partly financed by the expanding cosumer credit. The government consumption will grow slower that allows the control of fiscal deficits.
GROWTH TO ACCELERATE IN FIRST HALF OF 1997

As a result, we expect the economic growth to pick up from 4.2 percent in the third quarter of 1996 to about five percent in the following three quarters. However, the growth may start losing pace again in the second half of 1997. The further developments, particularly the foreign investment, may depend to a degree on internal and external political developments: the election outcome and the timetable for starting the EU accession negotiations (expected in the late 1997/early 1998).
ONE-DIGIT INDUSTRIAL PRICES INFLATION POSSIBLE IN 1997

Weakening indexation mechanisms, and particularly decelerating path of devaluation and falling inflationary expectations will result in continuous slowdown of industrial prices. The fall may be even stronger than we previously expected, pushing the growth of prices of manufacturing to a one-digit level already in the first half of 1997.

The reduction of the CPI inflation will be more uneven. Policy response to fluctuations in food prices was not efficient enough in 1996. As a result the CPI inflation is likely to exceed the government target and to exceed 19 percent in 1996. The fall of the inflation may be more impressive in the first three quarters of 1997 after the effects of the food market imbalances are finally absorbed. If this forecast materializes, significant interest rates cuts may be expected both in the first and second half of 1997.

NOTE: growth rates presented measure GDP growth in periods comprising four subsequent quarters (moving years) in relation to corresponding figures noted over the previous four quarters. The column for Q4 is an estimate for a calendar year. source:
